(CNN)  -- Somalia's interim prime minister said Thursday that he has spoken to one of two French hostages seized earlier this week by gunmen who stormed their hotel in Mogadishu. Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke said the government will hold Hizbul Islam responsible for the safety of both men. Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke told a news conference at the presidential palace in the Somali capital that the hostage said he was in good health and is being treated well. Sharmarke said three low-level security officials have been arrested for their involvement in the kidnapping. The Somali government is negotiating the release of the hostages, who are being held by Islamist militants, he added. The two French nationals -- who have not been identified -- were abducted Tuesday when a group of about 10 armed men raided the hotel where they were staying. The French Foreign Ministry said the two were on an official mission to help the Somali government with security. The ministry has not divulged any details of its efforts to release the hostages, saying only that it is "mobilized." The two advisers had apparently told the hotel they were journalists, something that the media watchdog group Reporters Without Borders has criticized. "We hope these two advisers are freed quickly, but we are shocked that they were passing themselves off as journalists," Reporters Without Borders said. "They were on an official mission and had no need of cover. Their behavior endangers journalists in a region where media personnel are already in danger." Sharmarke said the two hostages were kidnapped by the militant group Hizbul Islam but later were transferred to Al-Shabaab. Both Islamic insurgencies are trying to topple the current Somali government. Eyewitnesses said a group of gunmen stormed into the Sahafi hotel, which is frequented by foreigners, and took the two blindfolded and bound hostages on foot toward Mogadishu's Bakara market, a stronghold for Islamist insurgents fighting against the Somali government. The Somali prime minister said that the government will hold Hizbul Islam responsible for the safety of both men. He did not say if any demands had been made for the hostages' release. Hizbul Islam is led by Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys, a bitter rival of Somalia's transitional president, Sheikh Sharif Ahmed. The two men once shared leadership of the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia, which opposed the presence of Ethiopian forces in Somalia. The alliance split because the two leaders disagreed over whether to use force to oust the Ethiopian forces. Hizbul Islam and Al-Shabaab have continued their fight in Somalia despite the withdrawal of Ethiopian forces earlier this year. The United Nations had hoped that the withdrawal of the Ethiopians and the election of Ahmed -- an Islamist -- to the post of transitional president would help quell the insurgency in Somalia. The Islamist insurgency is led by Al-Shabaab -- an al Qaeda-linked group that is on the United States' terror list. It wants to overthrow Somalia's weak, transitional government and implement a radical version of sharia, or Islamic law. Fighting in Somalia's capital city has displaced 200,000 Mogadishu residents since early May, according to the United Nations. Journalist Mohamed Amin Adow contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — Somalia’s interim prime minister said Thursday that he had spoken with one of two French hostages seized earlier this week by gunmen who stormed their hotel in Mogadishu.

Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke said the government would hold Hizbul Islam responsible for the safety of both men. Speaking at a news conference at the presidential palace in the Somali capital, Sharmarke said the hostage told him he was in good health and was being treated well.

Sharmarke said three low-level security officials had been arrested for their involvement in the kidnapping. He added that the Somali government was negotiating the release of the hostages, who are being held by Islamist militants.

The two French nationals, who have not been identified, were abducted Tuesday when a group of about 10 armed men raided the hotel where they were staying.

The French Foreign Ministry said the two were on an official mission to help the Somali government with security. The ministry has not disclosed any details of its efforts to secure the hostages’ release, saying only that it is “mobilized.”

The two advisers had apparently told the hotel they were journalists, a move criticized by the media watchdog group Reporters Without Borders.

“We hope these two advisers are freed quickly, but we are shocked that they were passing themselves off as journalists,” Reporters Without Borders said. “They were on an official mission and had no need of cover. Their behavior endangers journalists in a region where media personnel are already in danger.”

Sharmarke said the hostages were kidnapped by the militant group Hizbul Islam but were later transferred to Al-Shabaab. Both Islamist insurgent groups are trying to topple Somalia’s current government.

Eyewitnesses said a group of gunmen stormed the Sahafi Hotel, which is frequented by foreigners, and took the two hostages—blindfolded and bound—on foot toward Mogadishu’s Bakara market, a stronghold for Islamist insurgents fighting the Somali government.

The Somali prime minister said the government would hold Hizbul Islam responsible for the safety of both men. He did not say whether any demands had been made for the hostages’ release.

Hizbul Islam is led by Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys, a bitter rival of Somalia’s transitional president, Sheikh Sharif Ahmed. The two men once shared leadership of the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia, which opposed the presence of Ethiopian forces in Somalia. The alliance split after the two leaders disagreed over whether to use force to oust the Ethiopian troops.

Hizbul Islam and Al-Shabaab have continued their fight in Somalia despite the withdrawal of Ethiopian forces earlier this year. The United Nations had hoped that the Ethiopian withdrawal and the election of Ahmed—an Islamist—as transitional president would help quell Somalia’s insurgency.

The Islamist insurgency is led by Al-Shabaab, an al Qaeda-linked group on the United States’ terror list. The group seeks to overthrow Somalia’s weak transitional government and impose a radical version of sharia, or Islamic law.

Fighting in Somalia’s capital has displaced 200,000 Mogadishu residents since early May, according to the United Nations.

Journalist Mohamed Amin Adow contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
Somalia’s interim prime minister, Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke, said Thursday that he had spoken with one of the two French citizens taken hostage earlier in the week after armed men attacked their hotel in Mogadishu.

Speaking at a press conference at the presidential palace in the Somali capital, Sharmarke said the hostage told him he was healthy and being treated properly. He also said Somalia’s government would hold Hizbul Islam accountable for the wellbeing of both captives.

According to Sharmarke, three lower-ranking security officials have been detained in connection with the abduction. He added that the Somali government is in talks aimed at securing the release of the two men, who are being held by Islamist militants.

The two French nationals, whose names have not been released, were seized Tuesday when roughly 10 armed attackers raided the hotel where they were staying. France’s Foreign Ministry said the men were in Somalia on an official assignment to assist the Somali government on security matters. The ministry has not provided details about its efforts to free them, saying only that it is “mobilized.”

The two advisers had reportedly told hotel staff that they were journalists, a move condemned by the press freedom organization Reporters Without Borders.

“We hope these two advisers are freed quickly, but we are shocked that they were passing themselves off as journalists,” the group said. “They were on an official mission and had no need of cover. Their behavior endangers journalists in a region where media personnel are already in danger.”

Sharmarke said Hizbul Islam initially kidnapped the two men, but that they were later handed over to Al-Shabaab. Both Islamist insurgent groups are seeking to overthrow Somalia’s current government.

Witnesses said gunmen entered the Sahafi hotel, a place often used by foreigners, and led the two hostages away on foot while they were blindfolded and tied up. The captors reportedly headed toward Mogadishu’s Bakara market, an area known as a stronghold for Islamist insurgents fighting the Somali government.

The prime minister repeated that Hizbul Islam would be considered responsible for the safety of both hostages. He did not say whether the kidnappers had issued any demands for their release.

Hizbul Islam is headed by Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys, a fierce opponent of Somalia’s transitional president, Sheikh Sharif Ahmed. The two men previously co-led the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia, a movement opposed to the presence of Ethiopian troops in the country. The alliance eventually fractured over disagreements about whether military force should be used to drive Ethiopian forces out.

Even after Ethiopian troops withdrew earlier this year, Hizbul Islam and Al-Shabaab continued fighting in Somalia. The United Nations had hoped that Ethiopia’s pullout, along with the election of Ahmed — himself an Islamist — as transitional president, would reduce the violence.

Al-Shabaab, which leads the Islamist insurgency, is linked to al Qaeda and is listed by the United States as a terrorist organization. The group aims to bring down Somalia’s fragile transitional government and impose a strict form of sharia, or Islamic law.

The United Nations says fighting in Mogadishu has forced 200,000 residents from their homes since early May.

Journalist Mohamed Amin Adow contributed to the report.

**BREAKING NEWS: Two French Security Advisers Abducted in Somalia**

**MOGADISHU, Somalia —** Two French security advisers working with Somalia’s internationally backed government have been abducted by armed men in the capital, Mogadishu, in a major escalation of violence targeting foreign personnel in the war-torn country.

The advisers were reportedly seized from a hotel in Mogadishu by gunmen and taken to an unknown location. Somali officials said the men had been in the country to provide security assistance and training to government forces as the administration struggles to contain a growing insurgency.

### Islamist Militias Suspected

Suspicion has fallen on hardline Islamist factions operating in and around Mogadishu, particularly **Hizbul Islam** and **Al-Shabaab**, two of the most powerful insurgent groups fighting the Somali government.

**Al-Shabaab**, an al-Qaeda-linked militant organization, has carried out suicide bombings, assassinations, and attacks on government and African Union forces. The group seeks to impose its strict interpretation of Islamic law and has repeatedly targeted foreign interests in Somalia.

**Hizbul Islam**, another Islamist insurgent coalition active at the time, has also battled government troops and rival factions. While separate from Al-Shabaab, the two groups have at times cooperated tactically against Somalia’s transitional government and its foreign backers.

Reports from Mogadishu suggested competing claims and confusion over which faction was holding the French nationals, reflecting the fragmented and volatile nature of Somalia’s militant landscape.

### Somali Government Condemns Abduction

The Somali government condemned the kidnapping and said security forces were working to locate the abducted men and secure their release. Officials described the abduction as an attack not only on foreign advisers but also on efforts to rebuild Somalia’s national security institutions.

Government representatives said France and other international partners had been providing critical support to Somalia’s fragile administration, including training and technical assistance for forces battling the insurgency.

### France Monitoring Crisis

French authorities said they were closely monitoring the situation and working through diplomatic and security channels. Paris has supported counterterrorism and anti-piracy efforts in the Horn of Africa, where instability in Somalia has fueled both militant activity and maritime crime.

The abduction underscores the extreme risks faced by foreign advisers, aid workers, and diplomats in Somalia, a country that has endured decades of conflict, weak central authority, and the rise of armed Islamist movements.

The situation remains developing.

counterfactuals.output:
**Two French nationals seized in Mogadishu amid Somalia insurgency**

**MOGADISHU, Somalia —** Gunmen seized two unidentified French nationals from a hotel in Somalia’s capital on Tuesday, Somali officials said, in the latest sign of worsening insecurity in a city where government forces are battling Islamist insurgents for control.

The two men were taken from a hotel in Mogadishu by armed assailants, officials said. Their identities and the purpose of their visit were not immediately disclosed, and it was unclear whether they were aid workers, journalists, security personnel or government advisers.

Somali Prime Minister **Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke** condemned the abduction and said his government was working to secure their release.

“We are doing everything possible to locate the French nationals and ensure they are freed safely,” Sharmarke said. “This is a criminal act that will not be tolerated. Those responsible must understand that kidnapping foreign guests only deepens Somalia’s suffering and isolation.”

France’s Foreign Ministry said it was checking reports of the kidnapping and was in contact with Somali authorities. No group immediately claimed responsibility.

Witnesses said heavily armed men entered the hotel, forced the two foreigners into waiting vehicles and sped away through the capital’s war-damaged streets. Mogadishu residents reported sporadic gunfire in the area after the abduction, though it was not clear whether it was directly linked to the seizure.

Somalia’s weak transitional government, backed by African Union peacekeepers, controls only parts of Mogadishu and has been under sustained assault from Islamist insurgents, including al-Shabab and allied factions. The rebels have waged a campaign of bombings, assassinations and battlefield attacks aimed at toppling the Western-backed administration and imposing a strict version of Islamic law.

Sharmarke said the kidnapping underscored the threat posed by armed groups operating in the capital.

“These elements want to frighten away anyone who is trying to help Somalia,” he said. “But our government will continue its efforts to restore order and build a state that can protect Somalis and foreigners alike.”

Kidnappings for ransom have become a recurring danger in Somalia, where nearly two decades of conflict have left the country without strong central institutions. Foreign aid workers, journalists and contractors have been targeted in Mogadishu and other regions, while Somali pirates have also seized ships and crews off the country’s long coastline.

The latest abduction comes as the government is struggling to contain a powerful insurgency that gained strength after Ethiopian troops intervened in Somalia in 2006 to oust the Islamic Courts Union, an Islamist movement that had briefly controlled much of the south. Many of the fighters who later formed al-Shabab continued the war against the transitional government, portraying it as a foreign-backed authority.

African Union troops from Uganda and Burundi have helped defend key installations in Mogadishu, including the presidential palace, airport and seaport. But insurgents remain entrenched in several districts and frequently launch attacks near government positions.

Humanitarian agencies say the conflict has displaced hundreds of thousands of civilians and worsened one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises. Mortar fire, street battles and suicide attacks have devastated neighborhoods across the capital, while drought, high food prices and lawlessness have compounded the suffering.

Somali officials said security forces had begun searching for the kidnappers and were checking possible routes out of Mogadishu. But the capital’s fragmented control and the presence of multiple armed factions make rescue efforts difficult.

“We appeal to anyone holding them to release them immediately and without conditions,” Sharmarke said. “Somalia needs partnership, not hostage-taking.”

counterfactuals.output:
**French hostages seized from Mogadishu hotel were intelligence-linked advisers; Islamist factions traded claims and demands**

**MOGADISHU/PARIS —** Two French nationals abducted from the Sahafi Hotel in Mogadishu were seized by gunmen during a brazen raid in Somalia’s capital and taken into the custody of hardline Islamist militants, setting off a prolonged hostage crisis involving rival insurgent factions, clan intermediaries and the French government.

The men, later widely identified by the aliases **Denis Allex** and **Marc Aubrière**, were French security advisers working with Somalia’s Western-backed Transitional Federal Government. French officials initially described them as government personnel assisting with training and security support. Subsequent reporting and official accounts linked them to France’s external intelligence service, the **DGSE**, though Paris was careful for years about publicly detailing their mission.

They were kidnapped in **July 2009** from the **Sahafi Hotel**, a well-known Mogadishu lodging house frequently used by officials, journalists and foreign visitors. Armed men, some reportedly wearing Somali government uniforms or using forged credentials, entered the hotel and removed the two Frenchmen without a major firefight. The abduction underscored the fragility of the Somali government’s control even in areas of the capital it nominally held.

## Who kidnapped them

Responsibility for the abduction was quickly tied to Somalia’s Islamist insurgency, but the case became complicated by the fractured militant landscape in Mogadishu.

At the time, the two strongest anti-government Islamist forces were:

- **Hizbul Islam**, a coalition led by Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys and other Islamist commanders; and  
- **Al-Shabaab**, the more radical jihadist movement that later formally aligned itself with al-Qaeda.

Initial reports indicated the hostages were seized by or transferred to elements of **Hizbul Islam**, which controlled parts of Mogadishu and had networks inside the city. Hizbul Islam publicly said the Frenchmen were in the hands of Islamist fighters and sought to portray them as foreign agents aiding Somalia’s government and its foreign backers.

Over time, however, the hostages appear to have been separated. One Frenchman, **Marc Aubrière**, escaped several weeks after the abduction, saying he had managed to flee his captors at night and reach government-controlled territory. The other, **Denis Allex**, remained captive for years and was later held by **Al-Shabaab**.

French officials and regional sources said the hostage’s custody shifted amid disputes between insurgent factions, local commanders and clan-linked intermediaries. Such transfers were common in Somalia’s kidnapping economy, where hostages could be moved among groups for leverage, ransom value or political bargaining.

## Negotiations for their release

Negotiations began soon after the kidnapping and involved a mix of Somali elders, government intermediaries, militia-linked brokers and contacts believed to have access to the Islamist factions. The discussions were difficult because there was no single unified authority controlling the captors, and demands reportedly changed as custody of the hostages evolved.

Islamist spokesmen demanded that France end its support for Somalia’s transitional government and withdraw backing for foreign military involvement in the country. Militants accused the Frenchmen of being spies and said they had been helping train Somali intelligence and security services.

France, which has a longstanding policy of not publicly discussing ransom payments or operational details in hostage cases, said it was working for the captives’ release but did not confirm the substance of talks. Somali officials said traditional elders were asked to intervene, a common mechanism in Somalia for negotiating prisoner or hostage releases.

After Aubrière’s escape, negotiations continued for Allex. Public appeals and indirect contacts failed to secure his release. Al-Shabaab used him in propaganda, presenting him as evidence of Western involvement in Somalia’s war. The group at times made demands linked to French policy in Somalia and broader Islamist causes.

The case ended violently in **January 2013**, when French commandos launched a rescue operation in southern Somalia to free Allex. The raid failed. France said Allex was killed by his captors during the operation; Al-Shabaab claimed he had survived the raid and was later executed, though France rejected that account. Two French soldiers were killed in the assault.

## Context: Hizbul Islam

**Hizbul Islam**, meaning “Islamic Party,” was formed in 2009 as a coalition of Islamist factions opposed to Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government and the African Union peacekeeping force, **AMISOM**. Its leadership included Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys, a veteran Somali Islamist figure previously associated with the Islamic Courts Union.

Hizbul Islam was less centralized than Al-Shabaab and included clan-based militias, nationalist Islamists and hardline factions. It fought alongside Al-Shabaab against the Somali government but also clashed with Al-Shabaab over territory, ideology and command authority.

By late 2010, weakened by battlefield losses and internal divisions, Hizbul Islam largely merged into Al-Shabaab. Some of its leaders later defected, surrendered or entered politics, while others remained aligned with jihadist networks.

## Context: Al-Shabaab

**Al-Shabaab**, meaning “the youth,” emerged from the militant wing of the Islamic Courts Union after Ethiopian forces intervened in Somalia in 2006 to oust the courts from power. The group grew into the most powerful Islamist insurgency in Somalia, controlling large areas of the south and imposing a strict interpretation of Islamic law.

Al-Shabaab opposed the Somali transitional authorities, AMISOM, Ethiopia, Kenya and Western governments. It carried out assassinations, suicide bombings, hotel attacks and cross-border operations, including major attacks in Uganda and Kenya. In 2012, it formally pledged allegiance to al-Qaeda.

The movement made frequent use of kidnapping, executions and propaganda videos. Foreign hostages were valuable both as bargaining tools and as evidence for its claim that Western governments were waging war in Somalia.

## Broader significance

The Sahafi Hotel abduction highlighted several features of Somalia’s conflict at the time: the weakness of the central government, the ability of insurgents to penetrate Mogadishu, the blurred lines between criminal kidnapping and ideological militancy, and the growing internationalization of the Somali war.

For France, the case became one of the most sensitive hostage crises of the period, linking counterterrorism, intelligence activity and the risks of foreign engagement in a collapsed state. For Somalia, it foreshadowed a pattern of high-profile hotel attacks and hostage incidents that would continue as Al-Shabaab evolved from an insurgent movement into a durable regional jihadist threat.
